problem: R2R agents depend on scarce human-annotated instruction-path pairs, and the speaker-generated augmentation data of Fried et al. is noisy: instructions often have little connection to the path they describe. Prior work used all of it without any quality assessment.
motivation: Paired vision-language navigation data is expensive to collect, so getting more from existing data matters. Environments make it cheap to build mismatched (negative) instruction-path pairs, which can train a discriminator that scores instruction-path fit and whose components can then initialize navigation agents.
key_idea: Train an alignment-based two-tower discriminator on cheaply mined negative paths (substitution, partial reordering, random walks) to score instruction-path fit. Use it to filter augmented data and to pre-train the navigation agent's encoders.
insight: Only a small, diverse, high-scoring subset of the augmented data is needed: adding the top 1% of the Fried augmented data to R2R train matches the benchmark SR (35.2 vs 35.5), and 5% exceeds it. Random sampling from the top 40% beats pure Top, so quality and diversity both matter. Curriculum training (PS negatives first, then PR and RW) raises discriminator AUC from about 72 to 76.2 and gives a visible diagonal alignment, whereas a PS-only model aligns only near the sequence ends. Encoder pre-training from the discriminator raises val-unseen SR from 36.0 to 39.1.
method: Two-tower discriminator: a BiLSTM instruction encoder and a BiLSTM path-visual encoder produce H^X and H^V.
Alignment score: A = H^X (H^V)^T, then a softmax over columns to pool each row, then a softmin over rows. This optimizes the best worst-case alignment between the two sequences.

Negative mining: keep the human instruction and alter the path by Path Substitution (other paths in the same environment), Partial Reordering (shuffle intermediate nodes) or Random Walks (share start or end, other end far away).
Curriculum training: first train on PS negatives only, then fine-tune on PR and RW negatives. Evaluated by AUC on PR and RW validation negatives.

Data selection: rank the Fried augmented instruction-path pairs by discriminator score. Train agents on Top, Bottom, Random Full, Random Top (top 40%) or Random Bottom (bottom 40%) fractions of 1%, 2% or 5%, alone or mixed with R2R train.

Discriminator initialization: retrain the discriminator with a unidirectional LSTM visual encoder and use its instruction and visual encoders to initialize the Speaker-Follower agent, then train with student forcing.

setting.backbone: Speaker-Follower-style agent (BiRNN instruction encoder with GloVe, LSTM visual encoder, panoramic action space) trained from scratch or initialized from discriminator encoders. The discriminator is a two-tower BiLSTM.
setting.training_data: R2R train, optionally with fractions of the Fried et al. speaker-augmented data. The discriminator is trained on R2R train positives plus mined PS, PR and RW negatives. Image features come from a CNN trained on a proprietary 100M+ image dataset.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views, 3 elevations x 12 headings) with CNN features and orientation features

numbers.extra: trained with R2R train and Fried augmented data; no beam search / pragmatic inference

results: An agent initialized from the discriminator reaches 39.1 SR on R2R val-unseen, versus the 35.5 Speaker-Follower benchmark (no beam search) and 36.0 for the authors' own re-implementation. The discriminator-selected top 1% of augmented data matches the benchmark SR (35.2 vs 35.5) and 5% gives 36.0. Val-seen performance drops with pre-training (SR 50.4 vs 51.9).
limitations: Val-seen performance drops with discriminator pre-training, and the authors' re-implementation is well below the benchmark on val-seen (SR 51.9 vs 66.4).
The discriminator's scores on val-unseen are conservative, and the encoder had to be retrained with a unidirectional LSTM, causing a minor degradation.
SPL does not improve with pre-training, gains are modest, and the image features are proprietary, which hinders reproducibility.
